newsitem.title: USA: Lawyer's emotional plea rivets Simpson civil trial.
newsitem.headline: Lawyer's emotional plea rivets Simpson civil trial.

text.p: A lawyer for the plaintiffs in O.J. Simpson's civil trial on Wednesday made an emotional appeal to the jury to force the ex-football star to pay compensation to the father of one of the murder victims.

Attorney Daniel Petrocelli stopped short of putting a figure on the amount he wants Simpson to pay Fred Goldman, whose son Ronald was murdered along with Nicole Brown Simpson in June 1994. Simpson was acquitted in October 1995 of the double murder but is battling a wrongful death civil lawsuit brought by the families of the victims, who are seeking substantial monetary damages.
"You can't put a value on the loss of a son, you can't put a price tag on it," Petrocelli said in closing arguments.

He said there would never be true justice for Fred Goldman. "True justice would be to see Ron Goldman walk through those doors right now, to see Nicole Brown Simpson playing with her children. That will never happen, they are gone forever."

Lowering his voice, Petrocelli, who represents the Goldman family, said there was nothing the jury could do to bring Ronald Goldman back. Then, turning and pointing his finger dramatically at Simpson, he said in a raised voice, "There is nothing he can do to bring him back."

"All you have in your power to do," Petrocelli told the panel of seven women and five men, "is to bring about some small measure of justice by requiring the man responsible to pay for Fred Goldman's loss."
During the emotionally charged end to Petrocelli's second day of closing arguments, Goldman and his daughter Kim sobbed quietly, as did Tanya Brown, Nicole Brown Simpson's sister.

While jurors tried to keep their composure, so strong was Petrocelli's delivery that some in the audience wiped away tears. Simpson looked uncomfortable and was reassured at one point by a defence lawyer who patted him on the shoulder.
"There is no loss greater than a parent losing a child. That loss is no less if the child grows into a young man," Petrocelli said.

Turning to the father-and-son team of Robert and Phil Baker, Simpson's two defence attorneys, Petrocelli went on, "We don't have to look beyond the counsellors' table to see the pride a father has for his son ... that is a pride Fred Goldman will have only in his memory."

He said Goldman would never see "the gleaming look of satisfaction on Ron's face as he ushered him into his new restaurant, never sit down at a July Fourth barbecue or a Passover or a birthday, never have the joy of going to the hospital to see his grandchild, a baby that Ron wanted to name Dakota."

After showing the jury one more time a video of Ronald Goldman and his father at a party less than a year before the June 12, 1994, murder, Petrocelli quoted 16th century poet Guillame du Bartas on the relationship between a father and son: "My lovely, living boy, my hope, my happiness, my love, my life."
Then, turning to the jury, he said: "Fred Goldman's lovely living boy is no more."

Petrocelli was followed to the lectern by John Kelly, the attorney for Nicole Brown Simpson's estate. He told the jury it had to make Simpson understand "that when he looks at photos of himself in the killer's shoes and says it's a fake, you're a liar. When you're unfaithful to your wife you're a cheater. When you kick her and pull her hair and beat her, you're a batterer. When you slaughter two people in the primes of their lives, you're a killer.
"All we are asking you to do is assign responsibility to the man who refuses to accept it," Kelly said.

Michael Brewer, who represents Ronald Goldman's mother, Sharon Rufo, told the jury, "You can tell O.J. Simpson: 'You killed two people, sir ... two people in the prime of their lives and, sir, they did not deserve to die.'"
Simpson's defence team was to begin its final summation later on Wednesday.
